:::{.callout-warning title="Note to reviwer"}

Below is the outline of the "story" of the paper. 

Intro:

1) TOBM (Total opioid burden metrics) are widely used (4,000 papers in 5 years and included in core outcome sets)

2) TOBM are not well defined, there is a number of conversion sets, calculators, and base units (OME vs MME)

3) TOBM arose from clinical practice but has since been used in research, describe history of conversions sets and calculators

4) There are potential issues with the metrics that have not been described before (dependance on proportion and error). Show how weighted sum of means = sum of weighted means.

Methods and results:

1) Show that there are dependences on proportion and error (red blue heatmap)

2) Show that these dependance are in clinical meaningful experiment space with a hypothetical simulation (red blue heatmap with subsection)

3) Show that the literature doesn't describe the metric methodology well (bar charts and heat map)

4) Show the across a range of reasonable assumptions, the results of a study can vary significantly (point and whisker plot)

Conclusion:

1) We have shown that TOBM is a metric that has inherent bias

2) This bias can change the results of a study by a significant amount depending on the situation

3) The features need to detect the bias (breakdown of mean dose and conversion values used) are not well reported by the literature

4) In the future we should:

	- Report the methodology of TOBM better
	
	- Aim to address the bias with improved conversion value estimates and statistical approaches to adjust for unbalanced groups.
	
:::

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

*Abstract to be written*

# Lay summary

In peri-operative research we use **opioid burden metrics** such as oral morphine equivalent (OME) or milligram morphine equivalent (MME) to pool the opioid dose across different opioids and routes for a patient. Often this pooled result is used to calculate group means and inter-group differences to estimate a treatment/associational effect. It is assumed that it doesn't matter which opioids are in each group as it is accounted for using the opioid burden metric.

We hypothesise that the differing opioids within the groups can bias the mean opioid metrics in un-equal ways between groups. We also hypothesise that if the conversion value is not exactly the same as the ground truth this will also contribute to bias.

We describe the equations used in practice and highlight their dependence on the proportions and error in conversion values. We then carried out a simulation to understand this relationship and demonstrate the bias introduced.

To establish the extent of the issue in research, we carried out a literature review to show how many studies publish their conversion metrics and intra-group medication proportions. We demonstrate that only a low percentage report both of the key aspects.

For papers that did supply the intra-group proportions, we simulated applying a range of different, but accepted, conversion values to demonstrate how the conclusions of the paper are dependent on the opioids used in each group.

We conclude that going forward all studies using an opioid metric must report the conversion values and proportions of medication within each group. We also call for new approaches to estimate conversion values that are offer a clearer view of the uncertainty involved.
